ratings.plot: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

verdict.reason: John Wilson's deadpan absurdism makes even a concrete documentary feel essential viewing. The joke—applying Hallmark workshop sentimentality to industrial materials—sustains itself through 100 minutes of genuine oddness.

ratings.plot: K2's first winter ascent claimed 5 lives, revealing modern alpinism's struggles with commercialization, social media impact, and conflicts between marginalized climbers and traditional elites.

verdict.reason: Amir Bar-Lev's documentary about K2's first winter ascent is essential viewing on the specific stakes of modern mountaineering. The film captures a real tragedy that exposes class fracture and commercial pressure in extreme sport, best witnessed in a theater where the altitude and moral weight can breathe.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A documentary about three doctors working across religious divides in Gaza demands to be seen while the crisis unfolds and the film is in theaters. Poh Si Teng brings journalists' discipline to a story where medicine and witness-bearing become the same act.

movies.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

ratings.plot: Follows Latif, a devoutly religious hitman, who embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children after his wife dies, confronting forces closing in and beliefs threatening to unravel.

verdict.reason: Bassam Tariq's follow-up to Srikanth shows a director deepening his command of action and character under pressure. The 35mm prints at Angelika and Lincoln Square give the Houston landscape and moral weight the scale they deserve.

ratings.plot: An archive-driven exploration of the life, work, and legacy of iconic, pioneering lesbian filmmaker Barbara Hammer.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip to see a major filmmaker's life and work documented with the rigor she deserves. Brydie O'Connor uses archival material to show how Hammer built an entire cinematic language from the ground up, and Film Forum is the right room for it.

movies.title: Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?

ratings.plot: Charting the Sheffield band’s extraordinary journey from obscurity to cultural touchstone. Fusing footage from Pulp’s biggest ever arena show – part of the global tour for ‘More’, the band’s first album in 24 years – with four decades of colourful, never-seen-before archival material.

verdict.reason: A band that defined the '90s returns after 24 years with new material, and this concert film captures both the reunion tour and four decades of unseen archives. The 99-minute runtime keeps the energy tight while the mix of recent arena footage and rare history gives you the full arc of a genuinely important British rock band.

ratings.plot: This film made by a Palestinian-Israeli collective shows the destruction of the occupied West Bank's Masafer Yatta by Israeli soldiers and the alliance which develops between the Palestinian activist Basel and Israeli journalist Y...
ratings.director: Yuval Abraham, Basel Adra, Hamdan Ballal

verdict.reason: This is essential documentary work made by Palestinians and Israelis together—rare, urgent, and shot from inside the conflict itself. Anthology's theatrical presentation of this restoration gives the images the scale they demand.

ratings.plot: San Francisco private detective Sam Spade takes on a case that involves him with three eccentric criminals, a gorgeous liar and their quest for a priceless statuette, with the stakes rising after his partner is murdered.

verdict.reason: Huston's debut is the template for every noir that followed—see it on the big screen before you see anything else. Bogart's performance is the reason the archetype exists, and the 100-minute economy of the script makes every scene count.

movies.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom

ratings.plot: On Halloween Eve at Mossy Bottom Farm, excitement turns to dismay when the clumsy Farmer ruins the pumpkin patch. Shaun tries fixing it with science experiments, but things go wrong when a wild beast appears in the woods.

verdict.reason: A stop-motion film that actually earns its theatrical seat with craft and charm instead of algorithm. The tactile texture and fluid character work are made for the big screen, not a tablet.

ratings.plot: Amy Goodman has reported some of the most consequential stories of our time. Steal This Story, Please. is a gripping portrait of a journalist whose unwavering commitment to truth-telling spans three decades of turbulent history.

verdict.reason: A sharp documentary about a journalist who built a career on stories the mainstream ignored, told by filmmakers with a track record of rigorous political work. The IFC Center is the right venue for this kind of cinema.

movies.title: Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger

ratings.plot: OASIS: DON'T LOOK BACK IN ANGER charts Liam and Noel Gallagher’s triumphant reunion tour, Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time. The film is an unapologetically uplifting account of the biggest musical event of 2025, capturing the experience and emotions of the band and their fans across the world. The unique perspective includes rehearsal, backstage, and onstage access as well as the first joint interviews with Noel and Liam in over 20 years. Alongside the band’s sold-out world tour, the film also explores the profound emotional impact of this phenomenal global cultural moment and what their music means to audiences and generations worldwide.

verdict.reason: See this on IMAX if you have any stake in the band or live music cinema. The format amplifies the scale of a reunion tour that mattered to millions, and the first joint interviews with the Gallaghers in over two decades justify the ticket price alone.

ratings.plot: Fifteen years after murdering his sister on Halloween night 1963, Michael Myers escapes from a mental hospital and returns to the small town of Haddonfield, Illinois, to kill again.

verdict.reason: One of the foundational horror films ever made—see it on a big screen where Carpenter's compositions and sound design still terrify. The simplicity of the premise and execution is the whole point, and it plays infinitely better in a theater than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: A New York City advertising executive goes on the run after being mistaken for a government agent by a group of foreign spies, and falls for a woman whose loyalties he begins to doubt.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's perfect thrillers and essential Hitchcock on the big screen. The crop duster sequence and Mount Rushmore climax demand theatrical scale.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan built this for 70mm and IMAX—see it at maximum scale or wait for home video. The format options across NYC are plentiful; catch it in the largest frame possible.

ratings.plot: After enduring years of malfunctioning products, Wile E. Coyote teams up with a local personal injury attorney to take on ACME, the manufacturer of anything and everything used by the Looney Tunes characters.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this on the big screen where the physical comedy lands hardest. Dave Green's direction turns a lawsuit gimmick into genuine slapstick theater, and 103 minutes of animated destruction plays best in a room full of people laughing at the same frame.

ratings.plot: At Westerburg High where cliques rule, jocks dominate and all the popular girls are named Heather, it's going to take a Veronica and mysterious new kid to give teen angst a body count.

verdict.reason: A bone-black comedy that invented the teen-movie-with-a-body-count formula and still owns the room. Michael Lehmann's direction has the snap of a snare drum, and seeing this restored on a big screen reminds you that dark satire about high school hierarchies ages better than the high schoolers themselves.

ratings.plot: In 2006, To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.

verdict.reason: Lance Oppenheim has made a sharp film about television, predation, and the machinery of public spectacle that demands to be seen on screen. The subject matter—how Hansen turned moral panic into ratings—cuts deeper than any true-crime procedural, and the theatrical experience lets you feel the manipulation in real time.

ratings.plot: In the antebellum United States, Solomon Northup, a free black man from upstate New York, is abducted and sold into slavery.

verdict.reason: Steve McQueen's unflinching direction and Chiwetel Ejiofor's performance make this essential viewing on a large screen. The compositions and long takes force you to sit with the brutality instead of looking away.

movies.title: If I Go Will They Miss Me

ratings.plot: A boy sees ghostly figures of other boys in his neighborhood while grappling with his father's distance. These visions uncover hidden connections between them and their shared heritage.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real poetry in a boy's search for connection across grief and estrangement. Thompson-Hernandez builds something rare—a ghost story that earns its supernatural language because the emotional weight underneath is genuine.

ratings.plot: Haru and Luis love competing in Tokyo's ballroom dance scene, but after tragedy strikes, Haru withdraws into isolation. When friends coax her back to the studio, she develops an infatuation with the new instructor.

verdict.reason: Josef Kubota Wladyka's direction brings genuine warmth to a story about grief and return, treating ballroom dancing as a language for emotional recovery rather than spectacle. The film earns its two hours through character and craft, not sentiment.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun makes films about obsession and image that demand the theater, and this one pairs psychological unease with genuine formal ambition. The 35mm print at Angelika is the only way to see it—35mm slashers hit different.

ratings.plot: After earning a licence to kill, secret agent James Bond sets out on his first mission as 007. Bond must defeat a private banker funding terrorists in a high-stakes game of poker at Casino Royale, in Montenegro.

verdict.reason: The best Bond film in decades—a genuine reinvention that ditches gadgetry for visceral action and emotional stakes. Daniel Craig's first outing rewrites the franchise rulebook, and the parkour chase and torture scenes hold their power on the big screen.

ratings.plot: A career bank robber breaks out of jail, and shares a moment of mutual attraction with a U.S. Marshal he has kidnapped.

verdict.reason: Watch this. Soderbergh's 1998 command of rhythm, color, and chemistry between Clooney and Lopez creates a crime film that moves like jazz, not a heist blueprint.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A sharp 71-minute documentary that earns its runtime without padding. Myron Levin's direction stays focused and lets the subject breathe.

ratings.plot: On a remote Scottish isle, siblings Isla and Sandy hunt birds and talk to mythical beings while fighting off outsiders. Their lives change when Daniel, an awkward official, arrives to relocate them.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real comedy in isolation, strangeness, and the collision between community myth and bureaucratic intrusion. Louis Paxton's command of tone and landscape—mixing deadpan Scottish humor with genuinely surreal moments—rewards full attention on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson captures the precise moment a restless kid becomes Bourdain, and the specificity of that origin story—set in a single Provincetown summer—makes it feel urgent and alive rather than dutiful. The film earns its runtime by letting kitchen chaos and human mess unfold at real tempo, which is how Johnson works.

ratings.plot: The Weight, portrays the life of Jung(Cho Jae-Huyn) who grew up as an orphan and was adopted into a family of only a mother and a son. Jung is now a hunchback man due to scoliosis and is a live-in mortician taking care of corpses ...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of a quietly devastating character study that earns its emotional weight through restraint and attention. Director Jeon Kyu-hwan builds compassion through observation rather than melodrama, and the film's refusal to sentimentalize its subject demands to be seen on a big screen.

ratings.plot: An armchair mystery in which the life of a reclusive academic collides with the story of a clandestine technology that can photograph the past.

verdict.reason: A high-concept mystery about time photography deserves the big screen, and Lincoln Center's presentation guarantees a clean print. The premise—reclusive academic meets impossible technology—hinges on image and performance, not exposition, so theatrical immersion matters.

ratings.plot: While seeking to cure himself of a curse, young warrior Ashitaka stumbles into a conflict between the people of Iron Town and Princess Mononoke, a girl raised by wolves, who will stop at nothing to prevent the destruction of her h...

verdict.reason: One of the greatest animated films ever made—see it on a big screen where Miyazaki's landscapes and action sequences demand to be experienced. The 133-minute runtime rewards full attention, and theatrical projection transforms the hand-drawn detail and color into something streaming cannot match.

movies.title: Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie

ratings.plot: New footage by Rushdie's wife shows his recovery path after the attack, capturing both physical healing and renewed hope. Based on his memoir "Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder.

verdict.reason: Alex Gibney documents a story of survival and resilience with access that matters—intimate footage from Rushdie's wife showing the aftermath most people never see. This is journalism that only works in a theater, where the weight of testimony demands your full attention.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones made a film about artistic resurrection that earns its modest runtime and modest premise through direction alone. Film Forum is the right venue for a work this attentive to the texture of creative life and the people who sustain it.

ratings.plot: A Black war hero is hired to find a mysterious woman, and gets mixed up in a murderous political scandal in 1948 Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Carl Franklin made a noir that actually understands its historical moment and its protagonist's interior life. Denzel Washington's performance carries the full weight of a man navigating racism while trying to survive a corrupt system.

ratings.plot: A collection of four Japanese folk tales with supernatural themes.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about visual storytelling—Kobayashi's use of color and composed space to build dread has no equal. Film Forum's 35mm print is the only way to experience the textures that make these ghost stories work.

ratings.plot: The discovery of a severed human ear found in a field leads a young man on an investigation related to a beautiful, mysterious nightclub singer and a group of psychopathic criminals who have kidnapped her child.

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterwork of American gothic belongs on the big screen, where the color palette and sound design hit with full force. The Alamo Drafthouse run is a gift—this is the kind of film that demands theatrical immersion and cannot be replicated at home.

ratings.plot: A secret military project endangers Neo-Tokyo when it turns a teenage biker gang member into a rampaging psychic psychopath who can only be stopped by his best friend.

verdict.reason: One of the defining animated films ever made—see it on a big screen where the hand-drawn detail and kinetic violence demand to be witnessed. Ôtomo's command of composition and pacing across 124 minutes remains unmatched in the medium.

ratings.plot: An idealistic porn producer aspires to elevate his craft to an art when he discovers a hot young talent.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for one of Anderson's finest ensemble pieces about American dreams and delusions. The 155-minute runtime lets the story breathe across decades while maintaining perfect pacing throughout.

ratings.plot: A man who has struggled personally has conflicts with his upwardly mobile lawyer brother and well to-do fiancee and is reluctantly to be the best man at their wedding.

verdict.reason: Burnett's debut is a rare theatrical screening of one of cinema's most vital examinations of class and family fracture in Black life. Film Forum's revival restores a work that vanished from circulation for decades and deserves to be seen in its intended format.

ratings.plot: A Juilliard-trained violist navigates the New York City freelance classical musician scene, playing gigs that often draw her into the personal lives of strangers, all while living in her oddball family's NYC apartment.

verdict.reason: A sharp, funny film about the actual economics and indignities of being a working classical musician in New York—not a feel-good music movie but a real one. The 78-minute runtime and brisk rhythm let the comedy land without overstaying, and Hagen's eye for the specific absurdities of freelance life beats sentiment every time.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Cameron's action blueprint still holds—this is essential theatrical spectacle that demands a big screen. The liquid-metal T-1000 effects and practical stunt work remain the standard for how to execute science fiction combat.

ratings.plot: Two death-obsessed sisters, outcasts in their suburban neighborhood, must deal with the tragic consequences when one of them is bitten by a deadly werewolf.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film that uses genre mechanics to say something real about female adolescence and rage. John Fawcett's control of tone—balancing dark comedy with genuine dread—makes this a rare werewolf picture that works as both genre exercise and character study.

ratings.plot: A brave girl and her friends must escape a kids television show.

verdict.reason: Casper Kelly makes horror from the uncanny logic of children's television, and at 96 minutes he knows exactly when to leave. The premise—kids trapped inside a TV show—works best seen in a theater where the screen becomes the trap.

ratings.plot: After being institutionalized in a mental hospital, Su-mi reunites with her sister, Su-yeon, and they return to live at their country home. But strange events plague the house, leading to surprising revelations and a shocking conc...

verdict.reason: Kim Jee-woon's layered psychological horror demands a theater's sound design to land its shifts between dread and revelation. The film's final twist punishes inattention—see it once, properly, on a big screen before the ending spoils itself online.

ratings.plot: A mousy romance novelist sets off for Colombia to ransom her kidnapped sister, and soon finds herself in the middle of a dangerous adventure hunting for treasure with a mercenary rogue.

verdict.reason: Zemeckis at his peak—a film that invents the modern action-comedy by treating romantic banter and jungle set pieces with equal craft. The playful chemistry and breakneck pacing make this a theatrical experience that rewrites itself every time you watch it.

ratings.plot: While passing through a vacation resort, a newlywed couple encounters a mysterious, strikingly beautiful countess and her aide.

verdict.reason: See it for one of the most seductive vampire films ever made. Kümel's visual approach treats blood and sexuality as elegant design elements rather than exploitation.

ratings.plot: A gay cabaret owner and his drag queen companion agree to put up a false straight front so that their son can introduce them to his fiancée's right-wing, conservative parents.

verdict.reason: Mike Nichols' timing and ensemble work make this comedy land harder on the big screen than it does at home. Nathan Lane and Robin Williams generate real chemistry, and the physical comedy rewards the theatrical format.

ratings.plot: Five friends head out to rural Texas to visit the grave of a grandfather. On the way they stumble across what appears to be a deserted house, only to discover something sinister within. Something armed with a chainsaw.

verdict.reason: One of the most influential horror films ever made demands to be seen on a big screen where Hooper's relentless pacing and raw craft hit hardest. The 83-minute runtime moves like a sprint, and the Alamo's theatrical presentation lets you feel every frame of its still-shocking viscera.

movies.title: Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai

ratings.plot: An African-American Mafia hit man who models himself after the samurai of old finds himself targeted for death by the mob.

verdict.reason: Jarmusch at his most stylish and philosophical, a film that refuses to move at anyone else's pace. The deadpan collision of samurai code and street-level crime has only deepened since 1999, and the Alamo's 35mm print will honor the film's deliberate, luminous framing.

ratings.plot: The spirits of a deceased couple are harassed by an unbearable family that has moved into their home, and hire a malicious spirit to drive them out.

verdict.reason: Burton's design work and Michael Keaton's manic performance have aged into a masterclass of early MTV-era visual comedy. The 92-minute runtime lets the jokes land without overstaying, and this is the kind of theatrical grotesquerie that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: In 1999, a race of she-aliens, the Kilaaks, brainwash Earth's monsters into attacking major cities, prompting a team of astronauts to stop the invaders while the monsters battle Ghidorah.

verdict.reason: The last great Showa-era kaiju spectacle and the most fun monster movie ever made. Honda and Fukuda pack 11 creatures into 88 minutes and let them trash Tokyo with anarchic joy.

ratings.plot: Four inner-city teenagers get caught up in the pursuit of power and happiness, which they refer to as "the juice".

verdict.reason: Ernest R. Dickerson's debut is a rare theatrical grip on '90s Black cinema that still moves—the camera work and ensemble energy demand a big screen, not a small one.

movies.title: The Oldest Person in the World

ratings.plot: A ten-year worldwide exploration tracks successive holders of the oldest living person title. A study of longevity transforms into reflection on time's flow, fate's unpredictability, and the joy of human existence.

verdict.reason: Sam Green's decade-long documentary is patient, inventive filmmaking that earns its philosophical weight through lived time rather than narration. The theatrical experience of watching ten years compress into 87 minutes rewards the big screen in a way a streaming release cannot match.

ratings.plot: The Dark Knight of Gotham City begins his war on crime with his first major enemy being Jack Napier, a criminal who becomes the clownishly homicidal Joker.

verdict.reason: Burton's vision of Gotham still holds—a genuinely dark, production-design-forward superhero film that refuses to apologize for its strangeness. Nicholson's Joker is unhinged in a way modern blockbusters won't risk, and the 35mm print at Alamo Drafthouse makes the intricate set work sing.

ratings.plot: In 17th-century France, Father Urbain Grandier's protection of the city of Loudun from the corrupt Cardinal Richelieu is undermined by a sexually repressed nun's accusation of witchcraft.

verdict.reason: Russell's baroque provocation demands the big screen, and this restored 35mm print is the only way to see it properly. The sexual hysteria and baroque production design exist purely to be overwhelming in a theater.

ratings.plot: A woman discovers the newly resurrected, partially formed, body of her brother-in-law and lover. She starts killing for him to revitalize his body and escape the demonic beings that are pursuing him after he escaped their underworld.

verdict.reason: Barker's directorial debut is a genuinely inventive horror film that earns its cult status through practical effects and wilful strangeness. See it in a theater where the sound design of chains and screams hits like it was meant to.

ratings.plot: A deadly entity from space crash-lands near a small town and begins consuming everyone in its path. Panic ensues as shady government scientists try to contain the horrific creature.

verdict.reason: Chuck Russell's remake is lean, practical creature horror that knows exactly what it is at 95 minutes. The practical effects hold up better than most 80s sci-fi, and this is the right format to experience the blob's relentless consumption on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A teacher visits the house of one of his students after the boy goes missing, only to have a horrifying excuse for his absence from school.

verdict.reason: Shimizu's original is leaner and meaner than the remake that followed, and at 70 minutes it hits hard without overstaying its welcome. The theatrical screening at Alamo Drafthouse is the right place to catch this foundational J-horror blueprint on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A council case worker looks for the relatives of those found dead and alone.

verdict.reason: A quiet, precise film about dignity in bureaucratic systems that earns its restraint through accumulated detail. Pasolini's patient direction finds grace in the mundane paperwork of death, making this a rare theatrical screening of a film that rewards full attention in a dark room.

ratings.plot: Berated all his life by those around him, a monk follows his dream and dons a mask to moonlight as a Luchador (Mexican wrestler).

verdict.reason: Jared Hess made something genuinely weird and tender here; Jack Black's commitment to the bit inside that lucha mask is worth the Alamo Drafthouse experience. Few comedies this sincere about passion disguised as silliness.

ratings.plot: A mysterious young drifter who calls herself Nomi Malone hitches a ride to Las Vegas, where she finds work as a stripper and sets about clawing her way to the top of the Vegas showgirls.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's masterpiece of American excess disguised as exploitation trash. The theatrical experience amplifies both the absurdity and the genuine critique of Vegas capitalism.

ratings.plot: As the deadline for a historic strike nears, UPS Teamsters across the United States navigate the challenges of building solidarity with their 340,000 co-workers. This film joins UPS workers across the country-a budding UPS driver ...

verdict.reason: Go see it; Yael Bridge's documentary captures labor organizing in real time with urgency and specificity that makes the stakes tangible. The film catches a historic moment while it's still unfolding, and IFC Center is the right room for it.

ratings.plot: Filmmaker Colette Ghunim takes her parents to find the ancestral homes in Mexico and Palestine that they had fled from decades earlier.

verdict.reason: A rare personal documentary about displacement and return that earns its emotional weight through the director's presence behind and in front of the camera. Ghunim's willingness to film her parents confronting decades-old grief gives the film an intimacy that justifies the theater trip.

ratings.plot: Exploding out of the AGFA vaults as a brand-new 35mm preservation, this 1990s kung fu fantasia from Hong Kong is a breathtaking combination of action, comedy, and cooking.

verdict.reason: A restored 35mm Hong Kong kung fu film from the 1990s mixing action, comedy, and cooking is exactly the kind of repertory find worth leaving home for. The AGFA preservation and theatrical print make this a one-time screening experience.

ratings.plot: David Lynch cemented his reputation as an uncompromising visionary with BLUE VELVET, one of the most controversial films of the 1980s, burrowing beneath the surface of idyllic suburban America to reveal a sinister underworld of sex and violence. After stumbling upon a severed human ear, a young college student (Kyle MacLachlan) becomes obsessed with investigating its origins and gets entangled with a nightclub chanteuse (Isabella Rossellini) and her psychopathic lover (Dennis Hopper). A masterfully eerie, depraved psychosexual nightmare and one of the greatest films of the 1980s. “Frank Booth is the role Dennis Hopper was born and chemically mutated to own. Sometimes David Lynch can teeter too far into the absurdity for absurdity's sake, but BLUE VELVET remains perfectly balanced as it dives into the dark, bizarre underbelly of society that lurks just below the surface of suburbia. It is also worth noting that BLUE VELVET, when screened in the first month of operation at the original Alamo, was the movie that inspired our strict no-talking policy.” ( Tim League, Alamo Drafthouse founder)

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterpiece demands the big screen and the communal dark—this is where the film's sickly beauty and ugliness hit hardest. Dennis Hopper's Frank Booth is a performance so feral and unhinged that it needs theater sound to land the full psychotic force.

ratings.plot: One of the most derided movies of the 20th century is also one of its most spectacularly misunderstood. The odd-couple tag team of Dutch provocateur director Paul Verhoeven (ROBOCOP, ELLE) and Sleazoid-Hungarian-American writer Joe Eszterhas (FLASHDANCE, SLIVER) first came together with 1992's BASIC INSTINCT, and everyone, including the financial backers and the producer/distributors of this movie, assumed lightning would strike twice for the duo with 1995's SHOWGIRLS. Universally panned by critics upon its initial release, people found the multi-tap combo of inane dialogue, wild over-acting, and extreme obscenity and grotesquerie to be just too much. Then the "so-bad-it's-good" crowd sunk their hollow claws into the movie, claiming it as one of the "best worst" movies of all time. To be sure, yes, this is a movie in which Saved By the Bell 's Elizabeth Berkley sets fire to her TV-star image by grinding her pelvis on Kyle MacLachlan's lap until he simulates sexual climax while Gina Gershon watches. She shoves chips into her mouth and reminisces about her days of eating and enjoying "puppy chow," between bouts of trying to make it as a Las Vegas showgirl "goddess." The assumption that critics and chuckleheads alike have made are that a) Verhoeven and Eszterhas weren't trying to make something with humor (they were), and b) that the surface story is meant to be taken at face value (it's not). Verhoemie don't play that. SHOWGIRLS is a complicated, satirical masterpiece that tests the audience's limits of empathy and challenges some basic assumptions about American dreams of celebrity, pokes at the artificiality of Hollywood glitz and glamour, and shines a light on the misogyny and dehumanization inherent in the entertainment industry, all while keeping the audiences on their toes as they try to know whether they should laugh, cry, or scratch their heads because there are random interruptions by chimpanzees and the fiercest dancing ever committed to celluloid. (Laird Jimenez)

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's satire of Hollywood misogyny and celebrity worship is sharper and more intentional than its reputation allows, and a theater full of people ready to argue about it is exactly where this film belongs. The Alamo Drafthouse screening gives you permission to engage with the film's deliberate provocation rather than dismiss it as accidental camp.

ratings.plot: Presented in Japanese with English subtitles Big dreams, a shared passion – on the ice, they call it love. After suffering a humiliating loss at the Grand Prix Final, Japan’s number one skater, Yuri Katsuki, is ready to hang up his skates for good. But when his idol and five-time champion Victor Nikiforov offers to be his coach, Yuri’s put on a trek for gold and to discover the true meaning of victory! Together, they’ll face skaters from around the world.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of a beloved sports anime that earned its fervent fandom with genuine emotional depth and technical animation craft. The subtitled presentation at Alamo Drafthouse venues guarantees the original voice performances and artistic intent.

ratings.plot: A few years after surviving the last demon apocalypse, Brodie is washed-up, broke, and stuck in small-town purgatory. The long-awaited sequel to Jason Lei Howden's 2015 cult classic promises more gore, more metal, and more head-banging chaos than the original.

verdict.reason: Jason Lei Howden returns with the same anarchic energy and practical gore craft that made the first film a cult favorite. The Alamo Drafthouse is the only place in the city showing this, and it's the perfect venue for a film built on audience noise and communal chaos.

ratings.plot: Presented in an English dub The mind-melting 1995 anime classic GHOST IN THE SHELL still hits like a cybernetic fist over three decades later. The manga-turned-movie accurately foresaw our 24/7 connected world, and it profoundly impacted sci-fi for decades to come; there would be no MATRIX (and so many more) without GHOST IN THE SHELL. When Section 9 agent Motoko Kusanagi is assigned to track down the hacker known as the Puppet Master, what begins as a standard investigation in near-future Japan quickly turns into something more complex, more bizarre, and more existentially thrilling. Amidst all the kick-ass anime action, there are deep examinations of the nature of gender, the meaning of identity, and a vision of a near-future world that is all too close to our own. With gorgeous animation, teeth-rattling action, and more ideas and mind-blowing concepts than entire seasons of some TV shows, GHOST IN THE SHELL thrills here, in its original cinematic form.

verdict.reason: A foundational sci-fi film that shaped everything from The Matrix onward belongs on a theater screen, not a laptop. The 1995 animation holds up; the dub is accessible; and Alamo Drafthouse's multiple locations make this easier than you think.

Amidst all the kick-ass anime action there are deep examinations of the nature of gender, the meaning of identity and a vision of a near-future world that is all too close to our own. With gorgeous animation, teeth-rattling action and more ideas and mind-blowing concepts than entire seasons of some TV shows, GHOST IN THE SHELL thrills here, in its original cinematic form.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing on the big screen; this 1995 film remains the template for intelligent cyberpunk cinema and demands theatrical restoration quality. The animation, sound design, and philosophical density reward a theater's image and audio over any home setup.

ratings.plot: On July 27, 1986, Queen performed the largest-ever stadium concert at the Népstadion in Budapest in front of 80,000 ecstatic fans. Now, this original concert film has been beautifully rescanned and remastered in 4K alongside a dynamic new audio mix, featuring many of Queen's favorite tracks – "Bohemian Rhapsody," "Crazy Little Thing Called Love," "I Want To Break Free," and "We Are The Champions." With three years to go before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first Western rock concert performed in a stadium behind the then-Iron Curtain. It was of such significance to the Hungarian authorities and film industry that a group of the country's top film cameramen and technicians were brought together to film it for posterity.

verdict.reason: A restored 4K transfer of the last major Queen tour with Freddie Mercury, shot by Hungary's top film crew at a landmark Cold War moment. The remastered audio and visual restoration justify the theatrical experience for one of rock's most electrifying performances.

ratings.plot: Mobilizing the full resources of the Ufa Studios, F.W. Gösta Ekman stars as the titular alchemist who, struggling with his faith amidst a devastating plague, is offered the power to cure and the gift of youth...in exchange for his soul. As the diabolical Mephisto, Emil Jannings (The Last Laugh) delivers a performance of operatic scale and intensity, by turns charming, comical, and horrific. movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari w/ Invincible Czars

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: Watch it. A 1920 expressionist landmark that shaped everything that followed, and live music transforms a silent masterpiece into an event.

verdict.reason: See this foundational vampire film on the big screen with a live band that earned its reputation by understanding silent cinema's rhythmic hunger. verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to Tykwer's visual excess and can forgive the bloated runtime that drains the book's dark momentum. The 147 minutes of baroque cinematography and Wagner-scored obsession work best as a home viewing where you control the pace.

ratings.plot: A reckless group of twelve-year-olds sets out on a mission to spend the rest of their lives at sleep-away camp. They'll just have to get past Bob - the camp's deranged, relentless, 50-year-old lifer counselor.

verdict.reason: The premise is funny enough to gamble on if you want something light tonight, but the execution is uneven and the joke may not sustain a full runtime. Michael Lewen's direction has charm in spots, but the film never quite commits hard enough to either the absurdity or the heart it's reaching for.

ratings.plot: A young girl new to a Catholic school befriends a coven of witches whom the other students either shun or fear. But when a powerful invocation goes wrong, the consequences could endanger their lives.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for '90s goth camp that hasn't aged well outside of nostalgia. The execution is uneven and it plays better as a streaming rewatch than a theater commitment.

ratings.plot: A violent police detective investigates a brutal murder that might involve a manipulative and seductive novelist.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's 1992 pulp is sleek, nasty, and fun in ways that feel genuinely transgressive, but it's also hollow beneath the surface seduction. The Alamo screenings honor its B-movie ambitions if you're in the mood for camp with edge.

ratings.plot: A woman and her daughter leave Mexico for a better life in America, where they start working for a family whose patriarch is a newly-celebrated chef with an insecure wife.
Kirsty is brought to an institution after the horrible events of Hellraiser (1987), where the occult-obsessive head doctor resurrects Julia and unleashes the Cenobites and their demonic underworld.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical trip unless you're a completist or want the social experience of a midnight crowd at Alamo Drafthouse. Clive Barker's sequel loses the first film's surgical control, and the 97 minutes feel bloated rather than dense.

ratings.plot: A mysterious woman, fashion designer by day and prostitute by night, is hounded by two men: a married father of two children and a sexually repressed preacher.

verdict.reason: Ken Russell's excess and Kathleen Turner's fearlessness make this worth seeing if you're game for 1984 provocation, but the film's sensationalism outlasts its insight. The Nitehawk screening captures the sleaze Russell intended, which plays better in a theater full of people than alone at home.

ratings.plot: Young driver, Speed Racer, aspires to be champion of the racing world with the help of his family and his high-tech Mach 5 automobile.

verdict.reason: The Wachowskis' pop-art fever dream is visually audacious but structurally chaotic, and the 135-minute runtime tests patience. Watch it on a big screen if you're curious about ambitious genre failure, but streaming at home lets you bail without sunk commute time.

ratings.plot: A worldwide epidemic encourages a biotech company to launch an organ-financing program similar in nature to a standard car loan. The repossession clause is a killer, however.

verdict.reason: Skip the multiplexes, but catch it at Alamo Drafthouse if you're in the mood for midnight-movie chaos and don't mind sitting through an uneven pitch. Bousman swings wildly between genuine visual invention and tonal whiplash, but the opera-horror-splatter hybrid commitment is rare enough to warrant one viewing in a room built for cult movies.

ratings.plot: Struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) lands a seemingly easy ghostwriting job with famous author Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), only to discover that the Crawford family has enough secrets to fill several bestselling thrillers. As she digs deeper into the disturbing autobiographical notes Verity has left behind, the line between fiction and reality starts getting seriously blurry, especially with Verity’s husband Jeremy (Josh Hartnett) in the picture. Based on Colleen Hoover’s bestselling novel and directed by Michael Showalter, VERITY is the kind of glossy, grown-up thriller that knows exactly how much fun it is to go off the rails.

verdict.reason: A competent Colleen Hoover adaptation with capable leads and enough twists to earn its runtime, but it lands as slick pulp rather than genuine thrills. The Alamo Drafthouse screening is built for a crowd that will eat the melodrama alive, which is half the appeal and half the reason to wait for home viewing.

ratings.plot: Presented in Japanese with English subtitles Come and join Crunchyroll for an exclusive sneak peek at the new October season, before it hits streaming. We will be screening select episodes of new seasons for the first time. A can’t-miss theatrical event!

verdict.reason: Skip the hype—you'll see these episodes on streaming in weeks anyway. The only argument is community and first-look novelty, which evaporates the moment they hit Crunchyroll.

ratings.plot: A tormented secret agent with emotional and psychological problems attempts to stop an international cyber attack. This dark emotional mystery intensifies as he is betrayed by those he trusts and loves.

verdict.reason: Neil Breen's films are singular experiences that reward midnight-movie audiences willing to embrace their unfiltered strangeness. This one plays at Alamo Drafthouse, where the communal atmosphere matters more than the film itself.

ratings.plot: The latest animated spectacle from the studio behind SHREK and HOW TO TRAIN YOUR DRAGON follows lifelong best friends Jo and Raissa on their last night together before graduation sends them in different directions. A mysterious portal drops them on Nakali, a fantastical island filled with creatures from the Filipino folk tales they grew up hearing. Getting home means facing a terrifying manananggal, a hapless weredog, and a pretty serious catch: they may have to forget each other to leave. Bring your best friend and see it on the big screen.

verdict.reason: The Filipino folklore angle and friendship-stakes premise have real weight, but a 109-minute animated film built on a farewell story lands harder at home than in a theater full of strangers. DreamWorks polish can't overcome the fact that intimate emotional beats don't need the big screen.

ratings.plot: Jessica Chastain plays both sides of motherhood in this unsettling supernatural thriller, as a loving mom and the terrifying presence that begins haunting her daughter’s home. Jay Duplass and Dichen Lachman co-star in a nightmare where the simple words “there’s someone in the house” take on a whole new meaning. And if a ball pit doesn’t already make you nervous, this movie may have some ideas for you. See it with friends, or bring your mom and have plenty to talk about on the way home.

verdict.reason: Jessica Chastain playing dual roles in a supernatural thriller has genuine craft, but fan-event screenings trade theatrical immersion for crowd noise and phone light. The Alamo Drafthouse crowd will be loud; if you want to hear the movie's unsettling sound design, catch it elsewhere.

ratings.plot: At Chester’s cottage, good behavior earns karaoke. Getting answers is a little more complicated. After a mysterious apocalyptic(ish) attack leaves them bloodied, disoriented, and unable to speak, Liam (Joey Bader) and Mel (Kaylee McGregor) take refuge in the English countryside. Their oddball host, Chester (Oliver Woolf), feeds them, helps them recover, and introduces a system of rewards: behave yourself, earn “nifties,” cash them in for hot-tub time and dance parties. Beyond the cottage, things are less nifty. But within it, a makeshift family is taking shape. While Liam embraces their new life, Mel grows increasingly curious about the world Chester insists is too dangerous to enter… In their feature debut, directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson mix deadpan comedy, sibling rivalry, and creeping unease in a coming-of-age story about people who have to grow up all over again. Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2026 Manchester Film Festival and the Narrative Feature Audience Award at Dances With Films LA 2026, this has the sort of sensibilities that fans of Yorgos Lanthimos and Ben Wheatley will adore… and it’s a natural fit as an Alamo Exclusive.

verdict.reason: Feature debut directors mixing deadpan comedy with creeping dread shows real promise, but an 88-minute runtime and premise built on mystery mean this lands harder with the right mood than as a guaranteed night out. The Alamo Drafthouse exclusivity and festival wins suggest this is worth catching in a theater with people who'll get it, but streaming will likely be fine if you're not committed to the vibe.

ratings.plot: A notorious prison, an invisible force starts killing inmates brutally, compelling enemy gangs and corrupt guards to work together as they try to survive the mounting bloodshed.

verdict.reason: Joko Anwar's prison-set horror-thriller hybrid has genuine genre craft, but the runtime and tonal shifts demand you're in the right mood for a violent, darkly funny Indonesian import. The Alamo Drafthouse showing honors the theatrical craftsmanship Anwar brings to gore and suspense.

ratings.plot: After a harrowing plane crash, a Special Forces officer and his combat dog find themselves stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness. Together, they are forced into a brutal fight for survival against the elements.

verdict.reason: David Ayer knows how to shoot action and animal actors, but a survival thriller lives or dies on whether you buy the emotional stakes, and this one feels thin. The 4DX format at multiple locations is the main draw if you want the wilderness buffeting to do the work instead.

ratings.plot: After a seven-year hiatus following the devastating loss of their beloved bandmate Chester Bennington, Linkin Park's remaining members struggle to find their way forward. Their shared history and enduring friendship, combined with the fresh perspective of two new band members, spark a renewed creative energy that leads them on a transformative journey of artistic reinvention. Following the band from intimate 2022 studio sessions through their explosive From Zero album release and concert in São Paulo, the film UNSHATTER weaves together rare vault footage, electrifying performances from sold-out shows, and candid interviews with band members and fans – capturing the raw, honest story of what it means to start over.

verdict.reason: Skip the theatrical run unless you need the crowd energy; this is a band documentary that works fine on a screen at home. The 107-minute runtime and concert footage don't demand a theater seat the way a live performance does.

ratings.plot: Shrouded in secrecy! Encircled by intrigue! The Mystery Machine promises to deliver cinematic treasures that span genres, countries, and tastes... only for those brave enough to enter. All shall be revealed only after the credits begin. Screening on select Mondays with discounted admission.

verdict.reason: The blind-screening format is a genuine theatrical gamble that demands commitment, but the discount price and Monday slot suggest this is a lower-stakes experiment than a full-price reveal. You're paying for the surprise itself, not a guaranteed film.

ratings.plot: 40 YEARS OF FUCKIN' UP is SPINAL TAP, but real. It's a film about the infamous, fairly unfamous, and beloved punk rock band NOFX. This is the unbelievable story about how a group of untalented, drug-addicted teenage punks somehow became the most successful independent band in history – and they did it haphazardly, entirely on their own.

verdict.reason: A chaotic, fun ride for NOFX devotees and punk history buffs, but the two-hour-plus runtime tests even true believers. The Alamo's beer-and-heckle atmosphere is the right venue for this kind of controlled mess, which matters more than the film itself.

ratings.plot: Street Fighters Ryu and Ken reunite when Chun-Li recruits them for the World Warrior Tournament. As they face a hidden conspiracy, they must confront each other and their past-or face destruction.

verdict.reason: A live-action fighting game adaptation has never landed, and this one carries real risk despite Kitao Sakurai's pedigree as a character action director. The two-hour runtime and tournament structure suggest theatrical ambition, but the premise hinges entirely on whether Sakurai can make hand-to-hand combat feel earned rather than choreographed spectacle.

ratings.plot: A daughter unravels her father's dark past after his body, missing for 36 years, is found at a horrific crime scene.

verdict.reason: Jordan Downey has made inventive low-budget horror before, but a crime-thriller hybrid about unearthed family secrets needs sharper execution than genre exercise to justify the runtime. The Alamo Drafthouse screening gives you a crowd and a bar, which helps sell the mood if the script doesn't.

ratings.plot: Follows Frances Haugen, a young Facebook engineer, who enlisted the help of Jeff Horwitz, a Wall Street Journal reporter, to blow the whistle on the social network's most guarded secrets.

verdict.reason: Sorkin's playbook of rapid-fire dialogue and structural precision fits the whistleblower-meets-reporter story, but the stakes feel domesticated at 112 minutes when the material demands either sweeping scope or intimate focus. The Alamo Drafthouse screens are standard multiplexes, so you're not getting theatrical value beyond a decent sound system.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: A curated surprise screening works best if you trust the programmer's taste and have time to spare on an unknown 86-minute experience. The appeal lives entirely in the mystery itself and the venue's atmosphere, not in any film you can research beforehand.

verdict.reason: Pedro Pascal carries a film about a musician's midlife reckoning with genuine depth, but the two-hour runtime and introspective pace work better on a smaller screen than in a theater seat. ratings.plot: Presented in an English dub When Jubei saves a young ninja woman from the unthinkable, he assumes that’s the end of it. To his surprise, it’s only just the beginning. Together, the two investigate the mysterious deaths of an entire village, which uncovers a conspiracy of demonic proportions. Getting closer to the truth, the demonic forces will stop at nothing to silence Jubei and his companion for good!

verdict.reason: The dubbed version loses the vocal performance work that makes this 1993 cult classic sing, but the animation still cuts hard on the big screen. At 94 minutes on a theatrical print, it's a lean watch—just know you're getting a compromise version of a masterpiece.

ratings.plot: In a village outside Beirut, a mechanic receives many visitors who need to repair their cars. He soon realizes that he not only has to fix their cars, but has to fix them as well.

See it if you trust Kassem's eye for character in close spaces; skip if you need more proof of concept before heading to Prospect Park.
